blocks.text: 1. Measurement framework
1.1 There is no single meaningful “gigawatt”

Accelerator TDP is the summed design power of chips. IT load includes host CPUs, memory, networking and storage. Facility load adds cooling, pumps, power conversion and redundancy. Utility or campus capacity can include spare blocks and non-AI loads. Treating these as interchangeable can overstate or understate comparable compute by 20%-100%. [S01,S02,S05-S11]

blocks.text: For fleet estimates based on accelerator TDP, the central bridge is facility power = 2.0x accelerator TDP and IT power = facility power / 1.25 PUE = 1.6x TDP. Sensitivity ranges are 1.7x-2.3x for facility/TDP and 1.18x-1.35x for PUE. [S05; Model]

Target-state sites are separate from signed contracts. A target may lack binding customer demand; a contract may be served across multiple sites. [S16-S34]
The site database estimates 46% coverage and reports material uncertainty. This report uses floors and ranges rather than false precision. [S01,S02]

blocks.text: 4.1 Amazon / Anthropic

Anthropic and Amazon announced an expansion above $100B over ten years for up to 5 GW of new AWS capacity. Nearly 1 GW of Trainium2/Trainium3 capacity is expected by end-2026, and Anthropic stated that more than one million Trainium2 chips were already in use. The hybrid ratio is above $2B/GW-year, but it is not a tariff because value is a floor, capacity an upper bound and the ramp undisclosed. [S24; Model]

Project Rainier was fully operational in June 2025 with nearly 500,000 Trainium2 chips and an expected expansion above one million. New Carlisle is the second-largest tracked live AI site at 910 MW IT. [S01,S25]
4.2 Google / Anthropic

Anthropic announced up to one million Google TPUs, tens of billions of dollars of services and well over 1 GW online in 2026. A separate announcement describes a 5 GW Google/Broadcom program beginning in 2027. Because overlap is undisclosed, this report shows 1 GW as a milestone and 5 GW as the program envelope rather than summing them. [S21,S22]
4.3 Microsoft: demand versus supply

Microsoft and Anthropic announced a $30B Azure purchase commitment and up to 1 GW of additional capacity. Separately, Microsoft contracted 200 MW IT from IREN for $9.7B over five years, approximately 200,000 GB300 GPUs from Nscale, and a $17.4B five-year GPU-services agreement with Nebius whose MW is undisclosed. Applying Nscale Texas disclosure of 240 MW for 104,000 GPUs to the total GPU count implies approximately 462 MW IT; a 700 MW option is excluded. [S16-S19; Model]

rows: Do not double count.  The 1 GW Anthropic demand commitment may be served by some combination of owned Fairwater assets and outsourced IREN, Nscale or Nebius capacity. Supply and demand rows are therefore separate. [S13-S19]

blocks.text: 4.4 Oracle / OpenAI and CoreWeave

OpenAI announced 4.5 GW of additional Oracle capacity, bringing the Oracle-linked program above 5 GW under development and above two million chips. A linked announcement referenced more than $300B and more than 5.5 GW; dividing those values produces a rough $10.9B/GW-year over five years, but it is not a clean tariff. [S33,S34; Model]

CoreWeave disclosed 1.5 GW active and 3.7 GW contracted, so the simple incremental bridge is 2.2 GW. Its $104B backlog divided by contracted capacity is $28.1B/GW, but duration and service mix vary. [S38; Model]
5. Footnote archaeology and capital commitments

Cash capex understates asset formation when finance leases, OEM financing, prepayments or JVs fund the build. Gross obligations can overstate AI exposure because they may include fulfillment, office, content, energy and general cloud assets. [S12,S20,S23,S27,S31,S37]
5.1 Microsoft

Microsoft reported FY2026 additions to PPE of $115.948B, net PPE of $313.076B and construction commitments of $34.566B. Total disclosed obligations were $743.821B, including $443.506B of leases including interest and $194.060B of purchase commitments. Uncommenced leases, mostly data centers, were $329.1B and begin FY2027-FY2033 with 1-20 year terms. RPO was $684B. [S12]
5.2 Alphabet

Alphabet spent $80.598B of first-half capex against $84.859B of OCF. Net PPE was $321.212B, including $122.814B of assets not yet in service. Uncommenced leases were $85.2B, primarily data centers starting in 2026-2031. Purchase commitments and other obligations were $811.0B; the filing also disclosed $24.1B of estimated data-center/energy backstops and $20B of private-company capital commitments. Cloud RPO was $513.9B. [S20]
5.3 Amazon

Amazon reported $98.411B of first-half cash PPE purchases against $71.419B of OCF. AWS net PPE was $263.750B and first-half AWS net additions were $90.120B. AWS RPO was $496B with a 6.4-year average duration. Amazon disclosed $137.214B of uncommenced leases and $650.034B of total commitments, but these totals include non-data-center categories. [S23]
5.4 Meta

Meta reported first-half capex including finance-lease principal of $50.920B against $64.088B of OCF. Net PPE was $225.724B and construction in progress $80.345B. Uncommenced leases were $278.99B at quarter-end; another $68B of data-center leases signed in July took the post-period figure to $346.99B. Contractual commitments were $349.31B; the totals likely overlap and are not added. [S27]

The Blue Owl Hyperion JV is an 80/20 structure covering approximately $27B of long-lived facility assets. Blue Owl contributed approximately $7B cash, Meta received a $3B distribution and Meta leases the facilities with a 16-year residual-value guarantee. [S29]
5.5 Oracle

Oracle FY2026 capex was $55.663B against $31.977B of OCF. Customer prepayments with a financing component contributed $4.592B to OCF; short-term capex financing added $3.345B and debt issuance was $46.093B. Net PPE was $99.957B and construction in progress $39.973B. [S31]

Oracle disclosed $260B of uncommenced leases, substantially all data centers, beginning FY2027-FY2029 with 15-19 year terms and including a $3.3B lessor guarantee. Other purchase obligations were $13.309B. RPO reached $638B. [S31,S32]
5.6 CoreWeave

CoreWeave reported net PPE of $46.736B and operating-lease ROU assets of $16.595B. First-half cash PPE purchases were $14.117B, while $9.796B of PPE liabilities/OEM financing and $8.359B of ROU additions were noncash. Uncommenced leases were $35.5B; one undelivered 393 MW site carried up to $14.7B of payments over 16 years. Debt principal was $35.551B. [S37]

CoreWeave had $103.7B of unsatisfied RPO in the 10-Q and approximately $104B of reported backlog; 1.5 GW active and 3.7 GW contracted. Its three largest Q2 customers represented 36%, 26% and 10% of revenue. [S37,S38]
6. Vendor dossiers
6.1 Amazon / AWS

rows: Q4 2025 model exceeds named-site floor [S01,S04,S05; Model]

blocks.text: AWS has the strongest vertically integrated named anchor: customer, ten-year minimum value, up-to-5-GW envelope and in-house Trainium roadmap. Trainium is approximately 41% of modeled Amazon H100e. [S04,S05,S24,S25]

The cost is cash intensity. First-half cash PPE exceeded OCF by 38%, and AWS added $90.120B of net PPE in six months. The Indiana program is $6.25B per disclosed data-center/facility GW and approximately $7.81B per modeled IT GW at 1.25 PUE. It is campus/infrastructure scope, not a clean full-stack accelerator bill. [S23,S26; Model]

rows: Stock implication.  At 20.9x, Amazon is not the most expensive hyperscaler despite the 5 GW anchor. The key test is whether Trainium lowers delivered cost enough to offset near-term negative free cash flow and whether the Anthropic ramp fills assets before refresh. [S23-S25,S48]

blocks.text: 6.2 Microsoft

Microsoft combines a large owned fleet with a broad outsourced network. IREN, Nscale and Nebius shift some construction, power and hardware financing to suppliers while reserving capacity for Azure. [S13-S18]

The benefit is speed and diversification; the cost is margin sharing and a complex stack. Microsoft had $329.1B of mostly data-center uncommenced leases and $743.821B of obligations, alongside $684B of RPO. [S12]

rows: Stock implication.  Microsoft has the best broad cloud demand visibility but trades at 30.2x, the highest P/E among the four hyperscalers. Its premium requires disciplined economics across owned and outsourced capacity. [S12,S16-S19,S48]

blocks.text: 6.3 Alphabet / Google

Google is the compute leader under both the chip-owner model and the site floor. Approximately 76% of modeled H100e comes from TPUs, creating the strongest custom-silicon position. H100e does not capture TPU workload fit or fungibility. [S01,S04,S05]

Alphabet has $122.814B of assets not in service, versus $247.177B of technical infrastructure in service. Cloud RPO is $513.9B, while the $811B broad commitment total makes the forward envelope less transparent. [S20]

The Hut 8 River Bend filing supplies a cleaner, though indirect, denominator: $9M-$11M per contracted IT MW for facility construction and a $7.0B 15-year base lease on 245 MW of IT capacity, equal to approximately $1.90B/IT-GW-year. A Google subsidiary backstops the contract; Fluidstack is the tenant, so this is not Alphabet-owned capex. [S49; Model]

rows: Stock implication.  Google combines the largest modeled compute base with the lowest P/E of the four hyperscalers at 17.0x. This is the strongest headline compute-to-valuation setup, subject to sustained TPU utilization. [S04,S05,S20,S48]

blocks.text: 6.4 Meta
Meta monetizes compute through recommendation, advertising and model capability rather than external cloud contracts. There is no independently priced tariff to validate unit economics. [S27,S28]

The balance-sheet strategy mixes direct construction, leases and Blue Owl JV financing. The raw $27B / 5 GW = $5.4B/GW ratio covers long-lived facilities, not servers, and scope/timing are mismatched. [S28,S29; Model]

rows: Stock implication.  Meta trades at 21.6x with strong ads cash generation, but post-period uncommenced leases equal 23.6% of market cap. Investors underwrite internal monetization plus long-lived lease and residual commitments. [S27-S29,S48; Model]

blocks.text: 6.5 Oracle

Oracle has the most concentrated public AI demand bet. The OpenAI program adds 4.5 GW and a linked >$300B commitment, creating exceptional visibility and exceptional sensitivity to execution and financing. [S31-S34]
FY2026 capex was 174% of OCF. Customer prepayments and debt funded the build, while $260B of uncommenced data-center leases equals approximately 60% of market cap. [S31,S48; Model]

rows: Stock implication.  Oracle offers the highest upside torque if capacity comes online on time and RPO converts at attractive margins, and the sharpest downside if power, construction, customer timing or financing moves adversely. [S31-S34,S48]

blocks.text: 7.4 Per-company cost per comparable IT GW

Per-company cost requires two lenses. The comparable engineering lens holds installed cost per IT watt constant at the Epoch base case—$37.883B upfront and $8.514B/year per IT GW—and applies each company's reconciled H100e density. The observed lens uses project, lease, hardware or service transactions and retains each transaction's scope. [S02,S03; Model]

Sources: compute [S01,S04,S05,S37,S38,S47]; common cost model [S02,S03]; future-capacity basis [S16-S24,S28,S33,S38,S47]; calculations [Model]. The future indicator is not uniformly incremental or signed.

On the common model, Google has the largest current replacement stack at $178.6B and the largest annual TCO at $40.1B. Meta has the highest current replacement-to-market-cap ratio among the four large hyperscalers at 6.1%. CoreWeave's modeled current replacement stack is $56.8B, or 121.5% of equity market value; debt and lease claims sit ahead of equity. [S03,S48; Model]

9.1 Hyperscalers

Alphabet has the best headline combination: the largest modeled compute fleet and the lowest P/E among Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta. Market cap per H100e is approximately $824,000, versus $1.08M for Microsoft and $1.15M for Amazon. Meta is lower at about $547,000 because its site floor is large relative to market cap, but capacity is internally monetized. [S01,S04,S05,S48; Model]

Microsoft deserves a premium for RPO visibility and enterprise distribution, but its 30.2x P/E and $329.1B uncommenced leases require strong utilization. Amazon has a lower 20.9x P/E and the strongest explicit vertical anchor but weaker near-term cash conversion. Meta's ads cash flows fund the build, while lease and residual commitments make its capital structure less asset-light than headline capex suggests. [S12,S23,S27,S48]
9.2 Oracle and CoreWeave

One modeled installed GW equals 8.7% of Oracle market cap and 81.0% of CoreWeave market cap, versus approximately 0.9%-2.6% for the hyperscalers. Incremental capacity therefore has much greater equity beta at Oracle and CoreWeave. [S03,S31,S37,S48; Model]

Oracle RPO is 147% of market cap and CoreWeave backlog 222%; these are exceptional demand indicators. Oracle uncommenced leases are approximately 60% of market cap, while CoreWeave debt and uncommenced leases are each approximately 76%. [S31,S32,S37,S38,S48; Model]
9.3 Scorecard

rows: Research conclusion.  GOOGL has the strongest current compute-to-valuation profile; MSFT the best broad cloud visibility; AMZN the strongest vertically integrated named anchor; META a strong funding engine without external tariff validation; ORCL the highest upside and financing torque; CRWV the purest and most levered public compute claim; TSLA compute is strategic option value rather than asset support. [S01-S05,S12,S20,S23,S27,S31-S38,S47,S48; Model]

blocks.text: 9.4 Replacement-cost bridge to equity value

blocks.text: 4.1 Amazon / Anthropic

Anthropic and Amazon announced an expansion above $100B over ten years for up to 5 GW of new AWS capacity. Nearly 1 GW of Trainium2/Trainium3 capacity is expected by end-2026, and Anthropic stated that more than one million Trainium2 chips were already in use. The hybrid ratio is above $2B/GW-year, but it is not a tariff because value is a floor, capacity an upper bound and the ramp undisclosed. [S24; Model]

Project Rainier was fully operational in June 2025 with nearly 500,000 Trainium2 chips and an expected expansion above one million. New Carlisle is the second-largest tracked live AI site at 910 MW IT. [S01,S25]
4.2 Google / Anthropic

Anthropic announced up to one million Google TPUs, tens of billions of dollars of services and well over 1 GW online in 2026. A separate announcement describes a 5 GW Google/Broadcom program beginning in 2027. Because overlap is undisclosed, this report shows 1 GW as a milestone and 5 GW as the program envelope rather than summing them. [S21,S22]
4.3 Microsoft: demand versus supply

Microsoft and Anthropic announced a $30B Azure purchase commitment and up to 1 GW of additional capacity. Separately, Microsoft contracted 200 MW IT from IREN for $9.7B over five years, approximately 200,000 GB300 GPUs from Nscale, and a $17.4B five-year GPU-services agreement with Nebius whose MW is undisclosed. Applying Nscale Texas disclosure of 240 MW for 104,000 GPUs to the total GPU count implies approximately 462 MW IT; a 700 MW option is excluded. [S16-S19; Model]

OpenAI announced 4.5 GW of additional Oracle capacity, bringing the Oracle-linked program above 5 GW under development and above two million chips. A linked announcement referenced more than $300B and more than 5.5 GW; dividing those values produces a rough $10.9B/GW-year over five years, but it is not a clean tariff. [S33,S34; Model]

CoreWeave disclosed 1.5 GW active and 3.7 GW contracted, so the simple incremental bridge is 2.2 GW. Its $104B backlog divided by contracted capacity is $28.1B/GW, but duration and service mix vary. [S38; Model]

5.1 Microsoft

Microsoft reported FY2026 additions to PPE of $115.948B, net PPE of $313.076B and construction commitments of $34.566B. 5.2 Alphabet

Alphabet spent $80.598B of first-half capex against $84.859B of OCF. Net PPE was $321.212B, including $122.814B of assets not yet in service. Uncommenced leases were $85.2B, primarily data centers starting in 2026-2031. Purchase commitments and other obligations were $811.0B; the filing also disclosed $24.1B of estimated data-center/energy backstops and $20B of private-company capital commitments. Cloud RPO was $513.9B. [S20]
5.3 Amazon

Amazon reported $98.411B of first-half cash PPE purchases against $71.419B of OCF. AWS net PPE was $263.750B and first-half AWS net additions were $90.120B. AWS RPO was $496B with a 6.4-year average duration. Amazon disclosed $137.214B of uncommenced leases and $650.034B of total commitments, but these totals include non-data-center categories. [S23]
5.4 Meta

Meta reported first-half capex including finance-lease principal of $50.920B against $64.088B of OCF. Net PPE was $225.724B and construction in progress $80.345B. Uncommenced leases were $278.99B at quarter-end; another $68B of data-center leases signed in July took the post-period figure to $346.99B. Contractual commitments were $349.31B; the totals likely overlap and are not added. [S27]

The Blue Owl Hyperion JV is an 80/20 structure covering approximately $27B of long-lived facility assets. Blue Owl contributed approximately $7B cash, Meta received a $3B distribution and Meta leases the facilities with a 16-year residual-value guarantee. [S29]
5.5 Oracle

Oracle FY2026 capex was $55.663B against $31.977B of OCF. Customer prepayments with a financing component contributed $4.592B to OCF; short-term capex financing added $3.345B and debt issuance was $46.093B. Net PPE was $99.957B and construction in progress $39.973B. [S31]

Oracle disclosed $260B of uncommenced leases, substantially all data centers, beginning FY2027-FY2029 with 15-19 year terms and including a $3.3B lessor guarantee. Other purchase obligations were $13.309B. RPO reached $638B. [S31,S32]

CoreWeave reported net PPE of $46.736B and operating-lease ROU assets of $16.595B. First-half cash PPE purchases were $14.117B, while $9.796B of PPE liabilities/OEM financing and $8.359B of ROU additions were noncash. CoreWeave had $103.7B of unsatisfied RPO in the 10-Q and approximately $104B of reported backlog; 1.5 GW active and 3.7 GW contracted. Its three largest Q2 customers represented 36%, 26% and 10% of revenue. [S37,S38]

Microsoft combines a large owned fleet with a broad outsourced network. IREN, Nscale and Nebius shift some construction, power and hardware financing to suppliers while reserving capacity for Azure. [S13-S18]

9.1 Hyperscalers

Alphabet has the best headline combination: the largest modeled compute fleet and the lowest P/E among Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta. Market cap per H100e is approximately $824,000, versus $1.08M for Microsoft and $1.15M for Amazon. Meta is lower at about $547,000 because its site floor is large relative to market cap, but capacity is internally monetized. [S01,S04,S05,S48; Model]

Microsoft deserves a premium for RPO visibility and enterprise distribution, but its 30.2x P/E and $329.1B uncommenced leases require strong utilization. Meta's ads cash flows fund the build, while lease and residual commitments make its capital structure less asset-light than headline capex suggests. [S12,S23,S27,S48]

One modeled installed GW equals 8.7% of Oracle market cap and 81.0% of CoreWeave market cap, versus approximately 0.9%-2.6% for the hyperscalers. Incremental capacity therefore has much greater equity beta at Oracle and CoreWeave. [S03,S31,S37,S48; Model]
